text.p: Computer maker Digital Equipment Corp. Thursday reported sharply lower profits for its second quarter, but the $31.9 million in net income beat Wall Street's expectations and the company's stock surged.
The profit, equal to 15 cents a share, represented a nearly 80 percent drop from the net income of $148.8 million, or 91 cents a share, the company posted in the last fiscal year's second quarter.
Industry analysts on average had predicted earnings of 10 cents a share, according to First Call, which tracks analyst estimates.

Digital's stock rose $3.50, or more than 10 percent, to $37.625 in morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange, making it one of the biggest gainers on the exchange. The stock was also among the most actively traded, with more than 800,000 shares changing hands.

The Maynard, Mass., company, which is a key supplier of business computers, generated operating revenue of $3.36 million for the quarter vs. $3.95 million in 1995's second quarter. The latest revenues were 15 percent higher than the $2.91 million recorded in its first quarter.

"I am satisfied with the progress the company demonstrated in the second quarter compared with our first-quarter results," company Chairman Robert Palmer said in a statement. "We needed to address a number of issues over the past few quarters to position the company for long-term growth. We are doing so."

Palmer said Digital's personal computer business unit generated a profit and met all its goals. "The personal computer business unit has done an excellent job meeting its goals over the past quarter," he said.
Palmer said the company's Internet software business unit had also done well.
Looking ahead, Palmer predicted that recent price cuts for the company's high-end AlphaServer and AlphaStation network computers and workstations would expand the market for the machines.

He also singled out for praise Digital's StrongArm microprocessor, which he said had been adopted by five companies for use in Internet or intranet devices. Intranets are internal corporate computer networks that function similarly to the Internet.
